claim_outcome_discrimination: First Respondent: discrimination claims allowed to proceed (time extended). Second and Third Respondents: discrimination claims dismissed for lack of jurisdiction (time not extended).
reason_for_out_of_time_unfair_dismissal: NA
reason_for_out_of_time_discrimination: The discrimination claims relating to incidents on 25 July 2023, 5 September 2023, and 6 September 2023 were presented out of time. The Claimant did not enter Early Conciliation with the First Respondent promptly after the alleged acts. For the Second and Third Respondents, Early Conciliation was entered into over one month later than for the First Respondent.
delay_reason: The Claimant stated she was waiting for the outcome of her Stage 3 appeal before contemplating any claim to the Employment Tribunal. She also said she received incorrect and conflicting advice from ACAS and was waiting for them to call her back before submitting forms for early conciliation against the Second and Third Respondents. She said she was confused at the time, did not believe she would be dismissed, was dealing with extensive paperwork regarding her appeal process, and relied on her disability as affecting her ability to present her claim in time. She also said her union representative did not provide advice and did not return her calls.
reasoning_unfair_dismissal: NA
reasoning_discrimination: For the First Respondent, the Tribunal found it just and equitable to extend time. The allegations were serious, the delay caused minimal prejudice to the Respondent and had limited effect on the cogency of evidence. The Claimant acted reasonably promptly to begin Early Conciliation once she received notification of the Stage 3 appeal outcome. She was trying to avoid litigation by exhausting the internal process. When taken with her vulnerability due to disability and the lack of or incorrect advice she received, it was just and equitable to extend time under section 123(1). For the Second Respondent, the Tribunal refused to extend time because Early Conciliation was entered into over one month later and the explanation (awaiting ACAS call back) was not convincing. The Second Respondent is not a legal entity and claims against it were unlikely to succeed as a matter of law. It was not just and equitable to extend time for claims with no prospect of success. For the Third Respondent, the Tribunal refused to extend time because the Third Respondent did not employ the Claimant, was only involved in the Stage 3 appeal, there was no claim of discrimination in relation to the Stage 3 appeal, and all allegations related to the First Respondent's conduct. Any claim against the Third Respondent would be likely to fail, so it was not just and equitable to extend time.
reasoning_factors_discrimination: length_of_delay; prejudice; disability; lack_of_advice; legal_advice_error; internal_appeal; acas_early_conciliation; promptness; merits
barriers_to_access: The Claimant stated she received incorrect and conflicting advice from ACAS. She also said that while she was technically represented by trade unions, her union representative did not provide advice and did not return her calls, only accompanying her to meetings. The Tribunal noted her vulnerability due to disability and the lack of or incorrect advice she received.
coding_notes: The decision clearly addresses time limits for discrimination claims under the just and equitable test and for non-discrimination claims (whistleblowing detriment and failure to allow accompaniment) under the reasonably practicable test. The Tribunal found all claims were out of time. For discrimination claims against the First Respondent, time was extended (just and equitable). For discrimination claims against the Second and Third Respondents, time was not extended. For non-discrimination claims against all Respondents, the Tribunal found it was reasonably practicable to present claims in time and refused to extend time. The Claimant was unrepresented at the hearing (in person) but had union representation during the internal processes. The decision does not specify exact delay periods in days. The discrimination type is clearly disability, as the Claimant relied on her disability and the decision refers to a disability bundle and reasonable adjustments claims.
positively_considered_factors_discrimina: prejudice; disability; lack_of_advice; legal_advice_error; internal_appeal; acas_early_conciliation; promptness

However, the tribunal found no basis to extend time. The Claimant had notified ACAS on 27 March 2024 (before receiving the emails), was represented by her Trade Union by early May 2024, and was supported by her husband. She participated in her appeal hearing on 8 May 2024. The tribunal found that the Claimant could reasonably have submitted her claim shortly after 11 April 2024 rather than waiting until 17 July 2024. Her explanation that it was a difficult time did not amount to a good reason, particularly given the support available to her. The tribunal noted there is a public interest in applying time limits strictly and that extension is the exception rather than the rule. While the tribunal found no significant prejudice to the Respondent (as the claim rested on three uncontested emails), this alone was not a reason to extend time.

The claimant did not start Early Conciliation until 1 December 2023 and issued proceedings on 9 February 2024, approximately six months late.
delay_reason: The claimant stated she needed time to think carefully and hoped to return to the respondent's employment after the requisite period. The tribunal found no reasonable explanation for the delay, noting the claimant was intelligent, literate, a union member, and had previously worked as an Employment Tribunal Clerk for seven months (August 2022 to March 2023), giving her unique knowledge of time limits.

The tribunal found no reasonable explanation for the delay, given the claimant's intelligence, union membership, and unique knowledge from working in an Employment Tribunal. The tribunal considered prejudice to both parties: the claimant would lose her claims, but the respondent faced prejudice from the passage of time affecting cogency of evidence (witnesses unable to recall events eight months later), and some witnesses had left employment and were reluctant. On merits, the tribunal found the claims weak: the claimant failed safety-critical tests three times in accordance with prescribed procedures; comparators were in materially different circumstances (Witness X raised menopause symptoms; others involved different misconduct); statistics showed 32 of 37 who failed tests were dismissed, including a broad mix by sex, race and age. The tribunal acknowledged that everyone subject to discrimination needs and ought to take time to think about what to do, and that the law provides three months for this purpose. The tribunal was less critical of delay during the period of Early Conciliation, though it noted this did not stop time as a matter of law because Early Conciliation was started after the three-month period had expired.

I have used 213 days as an approximate figure representing the period from 15 August 2023 to 9 February 2024 (date proceedings issued), which is the full delay period the tribunal considered. The tribunal explicitly rejected the claimant's explanation for delay, finding no reasonable explanation. The reasoning_factors for unfair dismissal include 'lack_of_advice' and 'ignorance_of_rights' but these are coded to reflect that the tribunal found the claimant had access to advice (union membership) and was not ignorant of her rights (Employment Tribunal Clerk experience), which weighed against her. reasoning_unfair_dismissal: The tribunal found that the claimant failed to establish that it was not reasonably practicable to bring the claim. Personal circumstances made it difficult but not impracticable. The tribunal did not accept that feelings of intimidation made it impracticable. The concepts of unfair dismissal and discrimination are well known and the claimant could have researched the point with reasonable diligence. The respondent did not mislead or inhibit the claimant. The claimant did not act promptly when she knew a claim could be brought. Even if it had not been reasonably practicable, the tribunal would have found that the claim was not brought in such further time as was reasonable.
reasoning_discrimination: The tribunal declined to extend time on a just and equitable basis. The claimant knew at all times that she could bring the claim. The triggering event in February 2024 demonstrated that the claimant chose to delay bringing her claim and proceeded at least in part because of her perception about the way others were treated. There was considerable delay. The passage of time could cause difficulties for the respondent in obtaining evidence, with relevant witnesses having limited memory or having moved on. The respondent did not contribute to any delay. The tribunal found that the claimant chose not to bring her claim but has now changed her mind. The tribunal rejected the argument that she had been inhibited by mental health, as it was not supported by adequate medical evidence and was inconsistent with her ability to work. The tribunal did not find it just and equitable to extend time.

barriers_to_access: The claimant stated she lacked adequate legal knowledge and understanding of the procedure for filing a tribunal case. She is a single mother and stated she lacks a support network. She referred to anxiety and depression. She was intimidated by the prospect of taking legal action for fear of potential repercussions and negative references. She was unaware of the legal costs and financial implications of bringing a claim. However, the tribunal did not accept these as making it impracticable to bring the claim or as justifying extension of time.
coding_notes: The delay length is calculated from the expiry of the primary time limit (16 April 2022) to the date the claim was presented (20 March 2024), which is 703 days. The tribunal applied both the reasonably practicable test for unfair dismissal and the just and equitable test for discrimination. The claimant's application for amendment was not decided as all claims were dismissed on time limit grounds. The tribunal noted that the claimant may not have two years' service for unfair dismissal but did not need to decide this point. The reasoning factors for discrimination include 'other' to capture the tribunal's consideration of the claimant's perception about generalised discrimination in the respondent company and her choice to delay bringing the claim.

coding_notes: This is a complex case involving extensive res judicata arguments. The tribunal's approach to the claimant's absence from the afternoon session and refusal to make oral applications/give evidence is significant to the outcomes. The case illustrates the intersection of res judicata principles, time limits, and strike out applications in the context of a litigant in person with disabilities.

claim_outcome_discrimination: The Respondent's application for strike-out and deposit order was refused. The discrimination claims proceed to final hearing. No substantive determination of the discrimination claims was made at this preliminary hearing.
reason_for_out_of_time_unfair_dismissal: NA
reason_for_out_of_time_discrimination: The Respondent contended that complaints based on events prior to 4 August 2023 were out of time. The Claimant's claim form was presented on 12 January 2024 following ACAS Early Conciliation from 3 November 2023 to 15 December 2023. The discrimination claims included: annual discretionary bonus payments (declared April 2019-April 2023), denial of Vice President status (January 2018-May 2022), and forcible transfer from GM, Crude to COEO (1 June 2022). The victimisation claims based on protected acts of 18 August and 18 October 2023 were accepted as in time. The Respondent argued that the pre-4 August 2023 claims were prima facie out of time and should be struck out.
delay_reason: The Respondent argued that the Claimant's claims relating to events prior to 4 August 2023 were out of time. The Claimant's case included arguments that: (a) the succession of bonus decisions were manifestations of a continuing discriminatory practice or policy amounting to conduct extending over a period; (b) unlawful decisions on bonus take effect when the deferred element is paid (in April following the declaration), rather than when the annual bonus is declared, meaning time ran from April following the relevant bonus declaration; (c) the bonus-based conduct extending over a period linked with the denial of Vice President status and the forcible transfer. The Claimant also raised mental health issues as a potential factor affecting the timing of the claim presentation, though this was not fully explored at the preliminary hearing.
reasoning_unfair_dismissal: NA
reasoning_discrimination: The Tribunal refused the Respondent's application to strike out the pre-4 August 2023 discrimination claims on time grounds. The Tribunal held that the Claimant had respectable arguments that: (1) the succession of bonus decisions were manifestations of a practice or policy motivated by discrimination and properly seen as conduct extending over a period under s123(3)(a) Equality Act 2010; (2) unlawful bonus decisions take effect when the deferred element is paid (April following declaration), meaning time ran from April 2023 for the April 2023 bonus, bringing claims comfortably within time; (3) if the bonus-based conduct extending over a period argument succeeded, the denial of Vice President status and forcible transfer claims could also be in time as further instances of the continuing discriminatory state of affairs. The Tribunal found the Claimant's case was nowhere near hopeless and had respectable arguments, falling very far short of having no reasonable prospect of success. On the just and equitable extension under s123(1)(b), the Tribunal held that even if the conduct extending over a period argument failed, the Claimant had reasonable prospects of persuading the Tribunal to exercise its broad discretion to extend time. Relevant factors would include: length of delay (which could not be determined at this stage and might be minor if time ran from April 2023); the Claimant's mental health (her case would need to be tested in cross-examination with medical evidence, but there was no reason to assume it would not be accepted); and prejudice to the Respondent (which could not be assessed without knowing the extent of delay). The Tribunal concluded the Respondent's arguments on just and equitable extension were even more difficult than on conduct extending over a period because there was no firm premise from which to start. The Tribunal emphasised it had made no factual findings and reached its conclusions without regard to oral evidence, applying the correct legal test for strike-out under rule 38(1)(a) of the Employment Tribunals Rules of Procedure 2024.
reasoning_factors_discrimination: conduct_extending_over_period; length_of_delay; mental_health; prejudice; effective_date_of_termination; merits
barriers_to_access: The Claimant raised mental health issues as a potential factor affecting the timing of her claim presentation. The Tribunal noted (para 54) that the question of the Claimant's mental health may be a material factor in considering a just and equitable extension, and that her case as to the extent to which that may have affected the timing of the presentation of her claim would need to be tested in cross-examination with medical evidence. The Tribunal also noted (para 2) that the Claimant went on sick leave in September 2023 and has not returned to work since, following the raising of a grievance in August 2023.
coding_notes: This is a preliminary hearing decision refusing the Respondent's application to strike out discrimination claims on time grounds and refusing a deposit order application. The Tribunal did not make a substantive determination of the time limit issues. The discrimination claims are partly out of time: victimisation claims based on protected acts of 18 August and 18 October 2023 were accepted as in time, but claims based on events prior to 4 August 2023 (bonus payments April 2019-April 2023, denial of Vice President status January 2018-May 2022, forcible transfer 1 June 2022) were argued by the Respondent to be out of time. The Tribunal held that the Claimant had reasonable prospects of succeeding on both the conduct extending over a period argument under s123(3)(a) and (if necessary) the just and equitable extension argument under s123(1)(b). The decision includes extensive discussion of the proper approach to strike-out applications versus substantive preliminary hearings on time limits, with the Tribunal holding that it should not hear evidence or make findings of fact at a strike-out hearing. The Claimant was represented by Ms D Romney KC and the Respondent by Mr D Martin KC. The decision also notes a pending amendment application delivered on 18 December 2024 which will be considered at a further preliminary hearing. Delay length in days cannot be calculated because: (1) the Tribunal did not determine when time began to run for the various claims; (2) the Claimant argued time ran from April 2023 for bonus claims (when deferred element paid), which would make them in time; (3) the extent of any delay depends on resolution of the conduct extending over a period argument, which was not determined.

His active steps to get advice and find out the position showed he was capable of also presenting his claim. The Tribunal applied Wall's Meat Co Ltd v Khan [1979] ICR 53, holding that ignorance or mistaken belief will not be reasonable if it arises from the fault of a claimant's solicitors or other professional advisers in not giving such information as they should reasonably have given. English not being his first language did not prevent him from researching and contacting multiple sources of advice.

Refusing the extension would deny the claimant the opportunity to put her claim forward in circumstances where the respondent was aware of the points raised.

coding_notes: The decision clearly distinguishes between the reasonably practicable test for unfair dismissal (refused) and the just and equitable test for discrimination (granted). Fourth, the claimant would be significantly prejudiced if not allowed to proceed, as disability issues are an integral part of her claims (the respondent allegedly did not adequately factor in her mental and physical health conditions when assessing performance).
